title: Committed sea-level rise under the Paris Agreement and the legacy of delayed mitigation action
problem: Existing sea-level rise assessments are often limited to the 21st century and older scenarios, failing to quantify the long-term (to 2300) sea-level rise committed by achieving the Paris Agreement's specific goals and the legacy of delayed near-term mitigation action.
method: The authors quantify sea-level rise until 2300 by combining a reduced-complexity climate model with a component-based sea-level model, which includes Antarctic ice-sheet instabilities, to assess stylized emission scenarios that fulfill the temperature and net-zero emission goals of the Paris Agreement.
task: The task is to quantify global sea-level rise until 2300 under Paris Agreement emission constraints, including the effects of Antarctic ice-sheet instabilities and the long-term consequences of delayed near-term mitigation action.

innovation: This paper quantifies committed sea-level rise until 2300 under Paris Agreement scenarios, revealing that each five-year delay in peaking CO2 emissions increases median sea-level rise estimates by approximately 0.2 meters and extreme estimates at the 95th percentile by up to 1 meter.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Some earth-system response features associated with falling global temperatures in net-zero GHG scenarios may not be captured correctly by the reduced-complexity model MAGICC. In particular, the hemispheric upwelling-diffusion ocean model may not comprehensively simulate the ocean response to sustained atmospheric cooling34. However, sea-level rise from ocean warming is calculated by the sea-level model and not directly by MAGICC in our approach.

For the three components, we use a pursuit curve approach, in which the difference between long-term sensitivity Seq(T,a) and the time-dependent contribution S(t) drives the rate of sea-level rise for each component: dS/dt = (Seq(T(t), a) – S(t))/τ

We use a response-function approach39, 40 for the Greenland solid ice discharge due to missing long-term sensitivity estimates or past trends in observations. This assumes that frontal stress release41 and runoff lubrication42 can be approximated as linearly depending on the global-mean temperature anomaly (ref. 18, equation 4).

Antarctic ice sheet: We apply a parametrization for Antarctic mass loss38, which incorporates increased sensitivity to global warming through two newly proposed instability mechanisms59. The mechanisms suggest a tight link between future atmospheric warming and Antarctic ice discharge19. The discharge thus also depends on the emission scenario. Our parametrization is calibrated to the results of ref. 19 and combines a slow and gradual response to global warming with a fast discharge term that mimics ice instability.
Thermal expansion: We estimate thermal expansion with the constrained-extrapolation approach following eq. 1, driven by the global-mean temperature evolution estimated by MAGICC16, 17.

We here explore the sea-level legacy until 2300 within the constraints of the Paris Agreement with a reduced-complexity carbon cycle and climate model ensemble16, 17 and a component-based simple sea-level model18. The sea-level model accounts for new evidence showing a higher sensitivity of the Antarctic ice sheet to global climate change19. We calibrate the Greenland component to newer observations that include the recent years of high-mass loss20, 21. We apply the methodology of ref. 18 without changes for thermal expansion and glaciers, which yield estimates similar to the IPCC AR5 for 21st century sea-level rise6.
